A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, eight figures, eighteen tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching content across appendix renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training experiments on likelihood displacement, CHES-based prediction, and safety refusal rates in Sections 3, 5, and 6, with further results in Appendix G.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results in Sections 3, 5, and 6 and the renumbered experimental Appendix H.

M1.justification: The CHES and length-normalized CHES definitions, data-filtering procedure, and preference-learning losses remain unchanged. The added fixed-embedding linear model is a theoretical case, not a revised proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions use Persona single-token agreement tasks, UltraFeedback and AlpacaFarm preference data, and SORRY-Bench refusal training and evaluation. No empirical dataset, domain, or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Section 5 retains normalized edit distance and last-hidden-embedding inner products as comparators. The refusal experiments retain unfiltered training, SFT regularization, and gold-preference comparisons, including their IPO counterparts. Newly cited research is not added as an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Table 1 broadens its stated qualitative criterion for catastrophic tokens from having an opposite meaning to having a meaning distinct from the preferred token. This is a limited revision to the reported categorization criterion; splits, training settings, numerical metrics, and generation parameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The supplementary experiments are retained through Appendix G becoming H: no-initial-SFT checks, IPO experiments, embedding-geometry and coefficient analyses, high/low-CHES examples, and refusal case studies. The separate training on response-pair types in Section 6.3 is also unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same ten-run single-token protocol with stable-run selection, three-run means and minimum/maximum plot error bars, and standard deviations in Tables 16 and 17. Seed and tuning-run information is unchanged.

E6.justification: Section 5 corrects the statement that preferred-response log probabilities under alternative similarity measures only increased: v3 acknowledges a few minor decreases. This better matches the retained Figure 2. Numerical table entries and plotted results, including the 74.4% to 33.4% refusal-rate drop, are unchanged.

T1.justification: New Appendix F adds Proposition 3, proved in Appendix G.9: with one prompt, single-token preferences, and a fixed hidden embedding, preferred-response log probability cannot decrease under the analyzed gradient flow. This adds a limited boundary-case result while retaining the principal theoretical analysis.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: catastrophic likelihood displacement, its embedding-geometric explanation, CHES prediction, and mitigation through preference-data filtering. The new appendix result does not redefine these headline claims.

C2.justification: Appendix C newly argues that the dispreferred-response squeezing effect is counteracted by the preferred-response gradient in the specified fixed-embedding linear setting. This sharpens the mechanism discussion and motivates analyzing evolving hidden embeddings. Section 8.1's substantive limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 Appendix I.3 explicitly identifies the SORRY-Bench judge model as used for refusal-rate evaluation; v1 Appendix H.3 specified only generation parameters there, although Section 6.1 already identified the judge for dataset labeling. This adds documentation without establishing an evaluator change. Hardware, hyperparameters, and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: Appendix C adds a substantive comparison with Ren and Sutherland's squeezing explanation. Section 7 expands discussion of online preference-learning guarantees with Zhang et al. and Xie et al.; additional bibliography entries cover adaptive-gradient dynamics and kernel-based finetuning. The overall research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized sentence and typo corrections, clarifies Takeaway 1, and updates conference-header and heading text. Inserting Appendix F shifts the former Appendices F–H to G–I, while the main section sequence and narrative are retained.

P2.justification: The ICLR formatting changes typography, heading appearance, header rules, spacing, and caption/table wrapping. All eight figures and eighteen tables remain, with the same plots and table structures; there are no added panels or redesigned result displays.

improvement.justification: The added boundary-case proof and accompanying mechanism discussion improve theoretical precision. Section 5 now describes the unchanged Figure 2 more accurately, and Appendix I.3 clarifies refusal-rate judging. These are useful, localized gains in rigor, accuracy, and reproducibility; the empirical evidence and central contributions remain essentially unchanged.
